title: Meaning of a set
subject: Mathematics
content: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The objects are called elements or members. Use braces to write a roster, for example A = {1, 2, 3}.

title: Roster notation
subject: Mathematics
content: Roster notation lists each element inside braces. An element is not repeated in a set; {1, 1, 2} represents the same set as {1, 2}.

title: Set-builder notation
subject: Mathematics
content: Set-builder notation describes members using a condition, such as {x in N : x is even and x <= 8}. Read the colon as 'such that'. Every listed member must satisfy the condition.

title: Domain matters
subject: Mathematics
content: In {x in Z : x squared = 9}, the domain Z means integers. Both -3 and 3 satisfy x squared = 9, so the set is {-3, 3}. Always read the domain and condition together.

title: Empty set
subject: Mathematics
content: The empty set has no elements and is written as empty braces or the empty-set symbol. For example, {x in N : 3 < x < 4} is empty because no natural number lies strictly between 3 and 4.

title: Singleton set
subject: Mathematics
content: A singleton contains exactly one element. The set {0} is not empty; it has the single member 0. Count members to distinguish it from the empty set.

title: Finite set
subject: Mathematics
content: A finite set has a countable number of elements and the count ends. The set {2, 4, 6, 8} is finite and has four elements.

title: Infinite set
subject: Mathematics
content: An infinite set does not have a finite number of elements. The integers continue in positive and negative directions. The real numbers in a bounded interval such as [0, 1] are also infinite.

title: Equal sets
subject: Mathematics
content: Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements. Order does not matter: {1, 2, 3} equals {3, 2, 1}. Check membership, not appearance.

title: Subset
subject: Mathematics
content: A is a subset of B when every element of A is also in B. To disprove A subset B, it is enough to give one element of A that is not in B.

title: Proper subset
subject: Mathematics
content: A is a proper subset of B when every member of A belongs to B and B has at least one additional member. A set is not a proper subset of itself.

title: Disjoint sets
subject: Mathematics
content: Two sets are disjoint when they have no common elements. Equivalently, their intersection is the empty set. Compare the actual members rather than the labels of the sets.

title: Union
subject: Mathematics
content: The union A union B contains every element that belongs to A or B or both. When writing a roster, include shared elements only once.

title: Intersection
subject: Mathematics
content: The intersection A intersection B contains only elements common to both A and B. If there are no common members, the intersection is empty.

title: Set difference
subject: Mathematics
content: A minus B contains elements that are in A but not in B. Start with A and remove any elements also present in B; reversing the order can produce a different result.

title: Complement
subject: Mathematics
content: The complement of A contains elements in the stated universal set that are not in A. The result depends on which universal set is being used.

title: Open interval
subject: Mathematics
content: An open interval (a, b) contains real numbers strictly between a and b. The endpoints a and b are excluded, shown by parentheses or open circles on a number line.

title: Closed interval
subject: Mathematics
content: A closed interval [a, b] contains both endpoints and every real number between them. Square brackets mean the endpoint is included, shown by filled dots on a number line.

title: Half-open interval
subject: Mathematics
content: The interval (a, b] excludes a but includes b; [a, b) includes a but excludes b. Translate each bracket separately instead of treating both endpoints the same way.

title: Interval to inequality
subject: Mathematics
content: The interval (-5, 9] corresponds to -5 < x <= 9. Parentheses translate to strict inequality and square brackets translate to an inclusive inequality.

title: Inequality to interval
subject: Mathematics
content: For 2 <= x < 7, the interval is [2, 7). Match the equality sign to an inclusive bracket and a strict inequality to a parenthesis.

title: Union of overlapping intervals
subject: Mathematics
content: If two intervals overlap or touch while covering every point between the outer endpoints, their union can be one larger interval. Confirm that no gap is left between the intervals.

title: Difference of intervals
subject: Mathematics
content: For A = [-3, 5] and B = (0, 6], A minus B is [-3, 0]. The point 0 remains because B excludes 0, while points greater than 0 are removed from A.

title: Cardinality of a union
subject: Mathematics
content: For finite sets, n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B). Subtract the intersection once because shared elements were added twice.

title: Three-set inclusion exclusion
subject: Mathematics
content: For three finite sets, add the three individual sizes, subtract each pairwise intersection, then add the triple intersection once. The pattern corrects over-counting.

title: Power set
subject: Mathematics
content: The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A, including the empty set and A itself. If A has n elements, its power set has 2 to the power n members.

title: Cardinality of power set
subject: Mathematics
content: A finite set with 3 elements has 2 cubed, or 8, subsets. Each element is either present or absent in a subset, giving two choices per element.

title: Cartesian product
subject: Mathematics
content: The Cartesian product A cross B is the set of ordered pairs (a, b) where a is in A and b is in B. Pair order matters: (a, b) is not generally the same as (b, a).

title: Count a Cartesian product
subject: Mathematics
content: For finite sets, the number of ordered pairs in A cross B is n(A) times n(B). If A has 2 members and B has 3, the product has 6 ordered pairs.

title: Check a proposed member
subject: Mathematics
content: To test whether a value belongs to a set-builder set, substitute it into the condition and check the stated domain. A value is included only if both the domain and condition are satisfied.

title: Check equality using membership
subject: Mathematics
content: To show two finite sets are equal, check that every element of the first appears in the second and every element of the second appears in the first. Equal size alone does not prove equality.

title: Common endpoint in interval union
subject: Mathematics
content: Intervals [1, 4] and (4, 7] do not both include 4, but the first interval includes it, so their union covers every point from 1 through 7. Draw a number line to check endpoint coverage.

title: Preserve equality when solving an equation
subject: Mathematics
content: To solve an equation, do the same permitted operation to both sides so equality is preserved. For 3x + 5 = 17, subtract 5 on both sides to get 3x = 12, then divide both sides by 3 to get x = 4. Check the result in the original equation.

title: Distribute a negative sign correctly
subject: Mathematics
content: A minus sign before brackets changes the sign of every term inside: -(a - b) = -a + b. For example, -(3x - 4) = -3x + 4. Expand each term, then simplify; do not change the sign of only the first term.

title: Add fractions with a common denominator
subject: Mathematics
content: For nonzero denominators, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd). Find a common denominator, convert each fraction, then add the numerators. Example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Do not add denominators directly.

title: Substitute a value using parentheses
subject: Mathematics
content: Replace the specified variable everywhere it occurs, keeping the expression's grouping. Parentheses help when substituting a negative value. If x = -2, then x^2 - 3x = (-2)^2 - 3(-2) = 4 + 6 = 10. Squaring -2 gives positive 4.

title: Apply a matrix row operation to the full row
subject: Mathematics
content: An elementary row operation acts on every entry in the selected row. For R2 <- R2 - 3R1, subtract three times each entry of row 1 from the corresponding entry of row 2. Valid elementary operations are swapping rows, multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar, and adding a multiple of one row to another row.

title: Calculate a two-by-two determinant
subject: Mathematics
content: For a 2 by 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad - bc. Multiply the main diagonal entries and subtract the product of the other diagonal. Example: det([[2, 1], [3, 4]]) = (2)(4) - (1)(3) = 5. The second product is subtracted, not added.

title: Keep the alternating signs in a three-by-three determinant
subject: Mathematics
content: Expanding a 3 by 3 determinant along the first row uses the sign pattern plus, minus, plus. For [[a,b,c],[d,e,f],[g,h,i]], det = a(ei - fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg). Compute each 2 by 2 minor carefully and keep the middle term negative.

title: Check units and dimensions before combining quantities
subject: Physics
content: Physical quantities can be added or compared only when their dimensions and units are compatible. In a valid equation, both sides must have the same dimensions. Multiplication and division combine dimensions, while adding metres to seconds is not meaningful. Convert units before comparing numerical values.

title: Check when a formula is valid
subject: Mathematics
content: Before using a formula, identify its conditions and the quantities it expects. For the quadratic formula, the equation must be in ax^2 + bx + c = 0 form with a ≠ 0 (that is, a is not zero). For a slope computed as change in y divided by change in x, change in x must not be zero. State the substitution and check that the conditions hold.

title: Explain why each step follows
subject: Mathematics
content: A complete solution gives both the operation and the reason it is valid. Name the rule or property, keep equality balanced, define symbols when needed, and connect the final result to the question. A correct sequence of calculations without the requested justification may be incomplete when reasoning marks are awarded.

title: Read the command word and constraints first
subject: Mathematics
content: Before solving, mark the command word (such as find, prove, compare, or state), the requested quantity, the allowed domain, and any conditions. A method can be mathematically correct but still not answer the question asked. Re-read the last line and check that the final response includes every requested part and its units when relevant.

title: Check arithmetic independently
subject: Mathematics
content: After choosing a correct method, reduce arithmetic slips by recalculating the key operation independently, checking signs and brackets, estimating the answer's size, and substituting a result back into the original equation when possible. Record a clear intermediate line so a reviewer can locate an arithmetic error separately from a concept error.

title: Union and intersection answer different questions
subject: Mathematics
content: The union A union B contains every element that is in A or in B (or in both). The intersection A intersect B contains only elements that are in both sets. For A = {1,2,3} and B = {3,4}, the union is {1,2,3,4}, while the intersection is {3}. Use membership in the sets to decide which operation is requested.
